risks: If `knowledge_links` is not called, document wikilinks are parsed but never stored in the index, so the planner remains blind to document-to-document and document-to-code relations.
`document_modules` and `code_modules` may be unused, meaning code-only consumers still iterate all modules including documents, potentially causing incorrect filtering or performance issues.

Determine if `_dedup_anchors` is needed; if not, remove dead code.
Audit consumers of `DocLink` to ensure `embed`, `alias`, `namespace` are handled appropriately.

report.summary: Adversarial review of vet.py gate. Identified 5 attack surfaces: (1) Unicode homoglyphs bypass exec.eval regex (e.g., 'еval' with Cyrillic 'е'). (2) Encoding tricks: UTF-16 or mixed encoding files may fail UTF-8 decode, producing UNSCANNABLE, but a file that decodes as UTF-8 with hidden homoglyphs passes. (3) Comment/string boundaries: inject.hidden_directive only catches HTML comments; Python or JS block comments can hide directives. (4) Acknowledgement mechanism: apply_allowances downgrades BLOCK to REVIEW for any subject/rule match; if allowances file is malformed, errors are returned but f
risks: Unicode homoglyphs in exec.eval pattern: Cyrillic 'е' (U+0435) in 'eval' bypasses regex because pattern expects ASCII 'e'. Same for other rules using \b word boundary.
Encoding tricks: A file that decodes as UTF-8 but contains homoglyphs passes scan_text; no normalization step exists.
Comment/string boundaries: inject.hidden_directive only matches HTML comments; Python triple-quoted strings or block comments can hide directives without triggering any rule.

Acknowledgement downgrade: If allowances file contains a subject/rule entry, BLOCK becomes REVIEW. A malicious skill could request an allowance for a rule it triggers, and if granted, the finding is downgraded to REVIEW, potentially bypassing human attention.
MCP server vetting: mcp.egress only flags hosts that appear in URLs; a server that resolves a host at runtime (e.g., via environment variable) is not detected statically.
No scanning of MCP server binary or its dependencies: only the command line is inspected; the actual server code is never scanned.
todos: Add Unicode normalization (NFKC) to scan_text before pattern matching to catch homoglyph attacks.
Extend inject.hidden_directive to also match Python block comments ('''...''') and single-line comments (# ...) with directive keywords.
Consider adding a rule for obfuscated exec patterns like '\x65val' or 'e' + 'val'.

Review allowance mechanism: ensure that acknowledged findings still require human review (currently downgraded to REVIEW, which is correct, but verify that REVIEW findings are not automatically cleared).
For MCP servers, consider requiring a hash of the binary or a pinned version to prevent runtime substitution.
Add a test suite that specifically tests homoglyph and encoding bypass attempts.

handoff.suggestion: The gate is well-designed with fail-closed principles, but content obfuscation via Unicode homoglyphs is a concrete bypass. Recommend adding a normalization step in scan_text: after decoding UTF-8, apply unicodedata.normalize('NFKC', text) before regex matching. This collapses homoglyphs to their ASCII equivalents. Also extend inject.hidden_directive to cover Python comments. For MCP servers, consider adding a rule that flags any command that is not a pinned local path (e.g., /usr/bin/python) as requiring review, since remote fetchers are already flagged but a local script could be swapped.

report.summary: The graph_delta module claims a multi-layer graph can detect defects missed by tests, but the measurement has critical flaws: (1) The mutation corpus is tiny (12 mutants) and hand-crafted, not representative of real defects. (2) Specificity is measured on the same repository's own history, which shares idioms and patterns with the mutation corpus, leading to overfitting. (3) The 'deleting direction' discriminator was derived post-hoc from the same data it is tested on, creating a circular validation. (4) Equivalent mutants (e.g., data literal changes) are explicitly invisible to some layers, b
risks: Mutation corpus is tiny (12 mutants) and hand-crafted, not representative of real-world defects.
Specificity measured on same repo's history; may not generalize to other projects.
Deleting-direction discriminator derived post-hoc from the same data it is tested on (circular).
No held-out validation set; risk of overfitting to the specific mutations and commits used.
Equivalent mutants (e.g., data literal changes) are explicitly invisible to some layers, but the claim of 1% false alarm rate is not supported by any data shown.
Specificity corpus limited to 80 commits, excludes merges; may not capture full distribution of real changes.
todos: Run specificity arm on a separate repository's commit history to measure false positive rate.
Increase mutation corpus size and diversity (e.g., use automated mutation testing tools).
Pre-register the discriminator rule (e.g., 'deleting direction only') before evaluating on held-out data.
Report confidence intervals or error bars on the 1% false alarm rate claim.
Document the exact commit range and filtering criteria for the specificity corpus.

handoff.suggestion: The measurement is not yet trustworthy. The key missing piece is a held-out specificity corpus from a different project. I recommend running the specificity arm on a popular open-source Python project (e.g., Flask or requests) and reporting the false positive rate. Also, increase the mutation corpus to at least 100 mutants using a tool like mutmut or cosmic-ray, and pre-register the detection rule before evaluating.

report.summary: Literature review on fitness signals cheaper than tests, novelty search descriptors, and the equivalent-mutant problem in GP and program repair. Key systems: GP (Koza, 1992) used raw test passes; TRACER (Fast et al., 2010) used test-case diversity as cheap signal; GenProg (Le Goues et al., 2012) used test passes; Prophet (Long & Rinard, 2016) used probabilistic model of correct code as cheap pre-test filter; DeepRepair (White et al., 2019) used AST structure similarity; novelty search (Lehman & Stanley, 2011) used behavioral descriptors like test-case output vectors; equivalent-mutant problem
risks: Graph delta misses control-flow-only changes (early return, condition inversion) as predicted and confirmed by literature.
Specificity arm not yet run; real commits may also show deletions, reducing discriminative power.
Equivalent-mutant problem not addressed; graph delta may treat semantically identical mutants as different.
todos: Run specificity arm on real commits to measure false positive rate.
Add control-flow layer (e.g., CFG edges) to catch early-return and condition-inversion defects.
Evaluate graph delta against equivalent-mutant detection methods from literature (e.g., dynamic invariants).

handoff.suggestion: Consider integrating a control-flow delta (e.g., CFG edge multiset) to cover the two missed defect classes. Also, run the specificity arm on real commits to measure false positive rate before using graph delta as a fitness signal.

report.summary: The promotion precondition chain in bootstrap.py is: (1) sources must be fresh (refresh_sources), (2) gate discrimination must be proven (gate_discrimination), (3) the gate must kill all critical defect classes completely, (4) overall kill rate >= 0.80, (5) the receipt must be bound to the exact gate being authorized (require_gate_binding=True). Currently false because: no discrimination receipt exists (DISCRIMINATION_REL_PATH absent), so gate_discrimination returns unproven; even if receipt existed, it must match current HEAD and the exact candidate gate. The shadow_run function never calls g
risks: gate_discrimination has no integrity protection on the receipt file; anyone writing runs/spine/gate_discrimination.json can forge a proven gate.
refresh_sources only refreshes the 'map' source; the 'inventory' source is not refreshed, so it may remain stale.
The shadow_run function does not call gate_discrimination with require_gate_binding=True, so even if a receipt existed, promotion_allowed would still be False because the binding check is skipped.
If _head_sha returns None (e.g., no .git), gate_discrimination now refuses, but the caller in shadow_run may not handle that gracefully.
todos: Add inventory source refresh to refresh_sources.
In shadow_run, call gate_discrimination with require_gate_binding=True and pass the candidate's gate configuration.
Add integrity protection (e.g., signature) to the discrimination receipt.
Ensure shadow_run handles the case where gate_discrimination returns unproven due to missing receipt gracefully.

handoff.suggestion: In daedalus/spine/bootstrap.py, modify shadow_run to: (1) call refresh_sources for both map and inventory, (2) after the attempt, call gate_discrimination with require_gate_binding=True and the candidate's gate config, (3) set self.discrimination to the result, (4) only allow promotion if discrimination.proven is True. Also add inventory refresh logic similar to map refresh.
